newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan opposition leader ready for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition leader ready for peace talks.

text.p: The leader of Afghan opposition forces besieging Kabul said on Monday he was ready for peace talks any time and anywhere, except Pakistan, to head off a bloody battle for the capital.

Northern Alliance leader Ahmed Shah Masood also made an impassioned plea in an interview with Reuters for the United States and other major Western nations to get involved in peace talks to repay what he said was a moral debt owed Afghanistan for helping to end the Cold War.

In written answers to a series of questions submitted by Reuters, Masood, a hero of the 1980s fight against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan, said he could take the capital whenever he wanted and oust Kabul's Islamic fundamentalist Taleban government.
Fighting has been in progress between the two sides for the past three weeks about 20 km (12 miles) from the northern outskirts of the capital.

"We are ready for talks with the Taleban without conditions under United Nations auspices at any place, except Pakistan, and at any time," Masood said. "We are ready to do this even though we are nearly at the gates of Kabul and have no reason to negotiate with them."
Opposition leaders say neighbouring Pakistan is directly helping the Taleban and wants to make Afghanistan a buffer state under its influence.

Masood said alliance plans to take over the capital had been temporarily put on hold while details were worked out for a civilian administration to run the capital and in hopes the Taleban would come to the negotiating table.
"There will also be a nationwide uprising against the Taleban in parts of the country they control in the next few days," Masood said. "We are coordinating our military actions in Kabul with this."
Masood proposed that if the Taleban agreed to talks, there should be a "temporary government formed for a very short time" that would set the framework and details of an elected government.
The temporary government would be formed out of a "loya jirga", or elders' council of prominent Afghans, both at home and abroad, that could include Taleban representatives.

Masood said the United States, a strong backer of his rebels during their fight against the then-Soviet Union's occupation of Afghanistan, should put pressure on Pakistan to stop supporting the Taleban.

"Our fight against the Soviets played a big part in breaking the Iron Curtain and ending the Cold War," Masood said. "We helped make the whole world safe from a nuclear holocaust and now the international community has forgotten and turned its back on us and our agony."
Some historians believe Moscow's failed incursion into Afghanistan accelerated the Soviet Union's economic decline, a key reason for the collapse of communism in East Europe.
